extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants and principal investigators (especially early-career investigators) seeking guidance on interacting with Program Officers and understanding peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical norms about how NIH Program Officers (POs) relate to peer review and how PIs should interact with them when preparing, submitting, and revising grant applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult POs early and often but integrate their advice
rubrics_metrics.description: "Talk to your POs early and often."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The blog endorses the usual advice to talk to POs early and often, but warns: "Do not take the PO word for gospel. Take it under advisement and integrate it with all of your other sources of information to try to decide how to advance your funding strategy." POs can occasionally be very helpful (e.g., select pay), but their input should be only one part of your decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat PO advice as definitive about review outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: "The NIH Program Officers do not completely understand what contributes to the review and scoring of your grant application."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PIs should be cautious about assuming a PO can predict scoring or fully explain study section dynamics. POs interpret reviews and can advise, but they do not have a definitive, omniscient view of how a study section will score an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: PO attendance at study section is inconsistent and limits insight
rubrics_metrics.description: POs often do not attend study sections in person and may only dial in for discussion of assigned grants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many POs don't attend in person (or only phone in for specific grants), they miss the broader discussion and context (e.g., comparisons to other applications) that drive scores. Lack of attendance contributes to their imperfect understanding of review dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: POs have variable helpfulness — evaluate PO by responsiveness and advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is wide variability among POs in engagement and utility to applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helpful POs are responsive, empathetic, attend or listen to reviews when possible, and may actively advocate (e.g., try to obtain funding via select pay). Other POs may be aloof, unresponsive, or out of touch; experience varies and luck of the draw matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: POs cannot speak during review and have limited direct power over study section decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: POs are not allowed to speak during review; they can only write a note to the SRO if they identify a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their formal role is to ensure ethical review and to interpret reviews post hoc; they have no authority to dictate study section scores or decisions. Even for RFAs they often lack power over the study section outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious when PO advice conflicts with study section feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not follow PO suggestions that contradict the study section's explicit feedback without careful consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post provides anecdotal examples where PO advice (e.g., changing a mentor) would have worsened funding chances despite positive study-section comments. If PO guidance diverges from reviewers' comments, weigh the risks and seek additional input.

rubrics_metrics.name: PO workload (number of assigned applications) affects the quality of their insight
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher application/PO ratios reduce a PO's ability to deeply follow and understand each grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments note POs may handle ~24 applications on average (or more), limiting time to attend and to know each application well. Applicants should consider PO workload when judging the depth of PO advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public tools (RePORTER) to identify POs and their portfolios before contacting them
rubrics_metrics.description: Search RePORTER for POs by keywords or name to see what grants are in their past and active portfolios and to learn their division/branch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommended workflow: identify likely PO(s) via RePORTER, review their portfolio/division description, email a short abstract and request a call, and then indicate in your application cover letter that you discussed the application with that PO/branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document PO interactions in your cover letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicate in the cover letter that the application "has been discussed with Dr. SoandSo and Suchandsuch Division/Branch at IC."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noting that you've discussed your submission with a PO is suggested as the best way to signal who your grant will be assigned to and that you have sought program-level input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish application aesthetics and clarity because program staff and reviewers manage huge portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: "Take your submission seriously even from the aesthetically point of view because portfolios exceed the 100s of grants... and is very, very difficult to master everything, and even read everything at times."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given the large volume of grants POs and staff must handle, clear, well-presented applications are easier to understand and more likely to be favorably considered when attention is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: POs' stated responsibilities and limitations — ensure ethical review rather than scoring prediction
rubrics_metrics.description: POs ensure there is no bias, study portfolios, identify gaps, review progress, and write initiatives, but they are "not here to tell you how will you score a grant."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the institutional constraints of POs: they provide guidance within policy limits, are liable for what they say, and cannot promise or guarantee funding. They may be strong advocates within those limits, but their role is not to guarantee outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: There should be institutional tracking of PO attendance and mechanisms for phone-in authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Grants Technical Assistant signs in/out POs for in-person attendance; phone-ins require PINs and likely are tracked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and commentators note that attendance should be recorded and that there are mechanisms (e.g., PINs) for phone participation; however, tracking phone attendance is harder. This affects how reliably you can infer a PO's exposure to study section discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train POs by having them review grants to improve their insight
rubrics_metrics.description: PO training should include reviewing grants to better understand study section dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests PO training include hands-on review experience (noting rules and firewalls may complicate this) to reduce disconnect between program staff and peer review.
